articles.headline: This Week in Charts: Agents Denied
articles.dek: Super-Pareto TikTok Shop; Cure to High Prices is High Prices; Zoomers Living Large?
articles.summary: Big retailers are blocking AI shopping agents, and surveys show most shoppers don’t trust bots to buy for them yet. Plus: TikTok Shop’s skew, chip prices and Gen Z’s finances.

cover.alt: A person holding a credit card while shopping online on a laptop

blocks.text: By Moses Sternstein
Agents Denied

Agentic commerce is a thing. Muse and others advanced the timeline to “agentic commerce is here right now—it was nice knowing you, old-school ecomm” but then more recently, some big etailers (like Amazon) responded, “not so fast—agent shoppers are officially instablocked.”

Now, the battle between what agents and bots can do vs. what the rest of the internet will allow them to do has been going on for some time, but the recent escalation does appear to show up in the data:
According to data from Cloudflare, the share of 403 “Forbidden” responses received by agents and bots has fattened considerably since the summer (and is ~double what it once was).

Whether that’s a response specifically to “agentic commerce” is a separate question, but presumably that’s at least some part of what’s going on. Etailers understandably don’t want to be disintermediated, and not only lose their customer relationships, but also lose those customer eyeballs that are a substantial source of advertising revenue for the large ecomm platforms.

There are likely other reasons why the Amazons of the world are apprehensive about agentic commerce, beyond simply eroding their platform advantages. First among those other concerns are likely fraud and returns, both of which have been a rising plague for ecomm more broadly:

According to data from the NRF, return rates and the total cost of returns have basically doubled and tripled, respectively, since 2019. Likewise, reported fraud is pervasive, with the most common concern being “dispute abuse,” i.e. customers buying something and then later disputing the charge. If the card issuer takes the customer’s side, the merchant is SOL.

It’s not hard to understand why etailers would be concerned that agentic commerce could make a worsening problem even worse. “Oh, my agent bought that personalized varsity jacket with my name in sequins, not me, I’d never do that” or “I told my agent to buy socks at the best price, but I didn’t expect it would find the ‘10,000 pairs of argyles, wholesale special,’ so please send a return label and a forklift.”

OK, so fraud, returns, customer relationships, and ad monetization are all throwing sand in the gears of the agentic commerce wave, but presumably those are solvable problems with better tech and commercial ingenuity.
There’s another problem, however, that may be holding back the bot-buying-spree: it’s possible that consumers don’t actually want their bots to do their shopping for them (yet).

As of now (according to some data, at least), consumers seem broadly open to the idea of AI helping them find what they’re looking for, and especially helping them find the best price, but when it comes to actually making the purchase, consumers appear to be somewhat resistant:

~25% of respondents said they’d be comfortable letting AI buy them a variety of consumer goods (except for luxury goods), but 42% said they would not trust AI at all to make purchases on their behalf. That’s less than half, but it’s still more than one would expect.

It would seem, that for now, consumers—like the etailers—are also worried about mistaken purchases, annoying returns, and chargeback disputes. That, and it may be the case that people just like to do their own shopping, at least when it comes to the final purchase decision.

Along those lines, there is some clickstream data from Similarweb (albeit a little stale) that seems to bear that out: AI is good for a consult, but buying is (for now) a human affair. There appears to be an increasing share of “shopping journeys” that visit AI before hitting the actual checkout page, but really the vast majority of AI shopping sessions appear to be in the “middle phase” of the journey, i.e. between discovery and purchase:

It’s fair to take this data with a grain of salt (because that is the nature of clickstream data), but the implications are otherwise pretty clear: for now, consumers seem to be using AI predominantly to do their homework on products they’ve already discovered, rather than either (a) discovering them with AI or (b) using AI to make the final purchase decision.

That makes the case for agentic commerce a bit less straightforward, but it especially makes the question of AI advertising attribution even less straightforward. If someone sees a recommendation in their AI-led middle shopping journey, but then makes the final purchase decision in a different session, then who will know what moved the consumer spirit to which outcome and when?

Again, the data appears to end in June, so whether that’s still true, let alone will remain true, is an open question, but either way, the relationship between shopper and bot is more complicated than it seems.
Super-Pareto TikTok Shop

While on the subject of ecomm, and potential disruption (or not) from agentic commerce, it turns out that social commerce on TikTok Shop has an incredible right-tail skew, for both the social part and the commerce part.
According to data from Marketplace Pulse, 8.4% of TikTok Shop sellers generate 1,000+ videos and capture ~60% of overall sales. Make a lot more videos, sell a lot more stuff.
But the distribution of sales to sellers is actually even more extreme.
Again, according to Marketplace Pulse, ~60% of sales are driven by the top 1% of sellers, and ~93% of sales are driven by the top 10%.
It’s hard to know what to make of this really, other than simply to marvel at the persistence of (super) pareto distributions, but Charts will try to, anyway.

• On the one hand, it seems that making a lot a lot of videos is a good way to drive sales, which implies there’s something evidently “personal” about the shopping experience that would be hard for an agent to replicate (although perhaps if Muse live-streamed its journey, that could change).

• On the other hand, if agentic commerce really does take off, then what would it mean for this small, but mighty cohort of prolific content creators who drive sales through a medium that has no relevance to an agent whatsoever?

Of course, agentic commerce and social commerce do not have to be mutually exclusive. Retail is really big, and there’s plenty of room for more than one model. But, it does seem broadly true that the way we shop now is optimized for a human interface to a degree that “just add agents” may be underestimating.
Cure To High Prices Is High Prices

Charts has no intention of weighing in one way or another on the “inflation: will it, won’t it” debate, but it will take a moment to reflect on the old saying that “the cure to high prices is high prices,” because it certainly seems worthy of some consideration.

The basic premise is straightforward: if prices get high enough, they suppress demand—either for that thing, or some other thing(s) that demand can no longer afford because demand is paying so much for the now more expensive thing. As everyone knows, when demand falls, prices tend to follow... so if high prices eventually suppress demand, and suppressed demand leads to falling prices, then the cure to high prices is... high prices.
Simple enough.
In this case, most everyone knows by now that AI capex has led to a surge in demand for chips and electrical components that is causing the price of those components to rise substantially:
According to the BLS, the prices paid for semis etc., by manufacturers of computers and computer-like things have skyrocketed over 25% YoY.
Now, those high prices do not appear to be dampening hyperscaler demand for chips—if anything, capex forecasts have gone higher, in part because the components have gotten more expensive.
But that doesn’t mean high prices are having no effect on demand. Hyperscalers may still be on a chip-buying spree, but everyone else appears to be saving their hardware upgrades for another day:
Just taking PCs as an example, according to IDC, PC shipments have dropped substantially since the beginning of the year.

It’s not just PCs that are facing some demand headwinds, but iPhones, as well, all of which have gotten more expensive, partly as a result of the AI buildout. Now, is it definitely the case that high prices are the reason that fewer PCs and iPhones are shipping? No, but it seems like a pretty good guess. And if that’s true, then the old adage appears to be working its way through the system (and will perhaps be reflected in softer prices, soon enough).
Consider, perhaps, another example of high prices being the cure to high prices.

Many, including the State of Markets, have observed the rising prominence of debt, when it comes to financing the buildout. Increased demand for borrowing (among other things) has, unsurprisingly, led to rising prices on that debt:
Rates for bonds linked to the tech sector have meaningfully diverged from the broader universe of corporate issuance, beginning roughly in September of ‘25, when capex borrowing began to take off.
More demand generally means higher prices, so it all checks out. And if higher prices eventually mean less demand, well, that too also appears to check out:

After growing substantially throughout the first half of the year, AI-linked debt issuance has fallen off since its June peak, with September issuance checking in at barely half of what was issued in August (which was already less than what was issued in July).

Of course, there are other reasons beyond supply and demand that would cause debt pricing to rise and fall, but supply and demand surely matter. And in this case, it appears as though the high price of borrowing has indeed put a damper on the inclination to borrow.
If demand falls, does that mean the cost of borrowing will fall in turn, and score another win for the old saying? We don’t know yet, but we’ll probably know soon enough.
Zoomers Living Large?
How’s this for a narrative violation?

According to some data and analysis from PNC Bank, Zoomers are actually doing pretty well, from a financial standpoint. Not only are they doing well, but Gen Z is doing considerably better in 2025 than Millennials were doing 10 years ago (when Millennials were Zoomer-aged):

Zoomers enjoy real incomes that are 20-40% higher than what their Millennial elders suffered at every part of the income distribution. Point-in-time generational comps are imperfect, but it’s still not the result most would expect to find.

It’s also not just higher incomes where Zoomers are winning. There’s also data that suggests Zoomers face lower unemployment, have higher net worths, more liquid assets, and bigger retirement accounts, then the previous generation did at an equivalent stage of life.
Indeed, with all that extra cheddar, it would appear as though Zoomers are living relatively large:
According to PNC’s internal data, Zoomers spend more of their income than Millennials and leave less in the rainy-day fund, as well.
In terms of what Zoomers are spending their money on, they allocate more to retirement, shelter, and transportation, and substantially less to education and energy:
At the category level, Zoomers also allocate relatively more to gambling and devices, but relatively less to clothing and sustenance.

Save more for retirement (but keep less in the rainy-day fund), while also hitting the tables and the money line, but sparing the booze. It’s an odd combination, but it’s Zoomer money, and they can spend it how they please.
Well, perhaps, “please” is the wrong word, because whatever their material advantages over generations prior, the Zoomer mood is decidedly dour:

Since 2017 (with a partial reprieve during pandemania), the traditional “sentiment” advantage that 18-34 year-olds typically enjoy relative to the broader population has all but evaporated. The Zoomers are not as cheerful as young folks of yore.

Now, consumer confidence is a very noisy series that has lost even more signal since the pandemic, likely because of falling response rates (among other things), but even if it’s noisier, it’s strange (but possible) that the noise would be isolated to 18-34 year-olds. In other words, even if the headline “confidence” figure is less reliable, one would think the ratios within ought to stay relatively stable... and in this case, it appears they haven’t: Zoomers are no more confident than anyone else, which makes them unlike all the young people of generations prior (at least through the ‘70s).

Taking this at face value, it would appear that the data does validate the vibe... but however bad the vibes may be, it’s hard to blame finances. That doesn’t mean Zoomers are without other reasons to feel relatively less optimistic, but certainly when it comes to making and spending money, they seem to be doing just fine.
Why so serious, Young Zoomer?
Source: a16z — https://www.a16z.news/p/this-week-in-charts-agents-denied

articles.headline: Made in China: Chinese manufacturing dominance may have only just started
articles.dek: China used to be known as the world’s factory. This era of Made in China may be harder to dislodge.
articles.summary: DAO Insights argues China’s factory edge is shifting from cheap labour to automation, AI and dense supply chains, and that it may next export machinery and know-how, not just goods.

cover.alt: Workers at a production line inside a Chinese factory
cover.credit: Photo: Truckrun / Unsplash, via DAO Insights

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• China’s manufacturing advantage is shifting from cheap labour to automation, engineering expertise and deeply connected supply chains
• AI could strengthen that advantage, but smarter factories still need demand: producing more does not guarantee profitable growth
• China could expand its influence by exporting machinery and manufacturing expertise, alongside finished products

In the 90s and early 2000s Made in China was stamped across anything cheap and mass produced. The label filled western clothing rails with fast fashion. Families ran on the help of inexpensive white goods. As a child, it kept me well-stocked in cheap toys.

For that era of Made in China, I wasn’t old enough to consider economics. Those that were assumed Chinese wages would eventually increase and the market would find a new place for production on the cheap. That would be the end of China as a manufacturing power.

The assumption lasts, as does the perception that all China makes is cheap and low quality. But what the country has learnt in the decades since the turn of the century has set it up to become a manufacturing hub of a very different kind, and one that will not easily be dislodged by market forces.
The factory becomes the next AI frontier

China’s factories of today are very different to the ones of old. They are high-tech and highly automated, producing very complex products like EVs, renewable energy systems and advanced batteries. China even manufactures the kind of tech that powers manufacturing this advanced.

Morgan Stanley estimates that China could invest up to $12 trillion through 2035 in infrastructure, factory upgrades and new industrial capacity. Its outlook envisages AI coordinating production, predicting maintenance needs and adjusting factory operations in real time.
These are expectations for an emerging industrial model, rather than a description of every Chinese factory today. But looking at what’s happening today doesn’t dampen China’s prospects either

High-tech manufacturing value rose 13.3% year on year in the first half of 2026, sending tech company profits flying by over 54%. Plus, China is beginning to pull away in global tech. 65% of the world’s EV batteries have the Made in China stamp, and over half of all industrial robots installed on Earth have it too. Interestingly, the old manufacturing base matters a lot to these industries.

China’s massive manufacturing scale and its tight supply chains produced strong engineering talent in its time at the low end of manufacturing. Then there’s the feedback loop. Because China has been producing for the world, its engineers run into factory problems – and solve them – more regularly, and faster than anyone else.
Ultimately, China’s industrial legacy leaves it with a wealth of practical expertise. As cheap labor fades, automation and productivity-boosting tech have become the new gold mine.
Smart factories still need customers

blocks.caption: Image: Unsplash/runda choo

blocks.text: Am I being over optimistic? Maybe. Even the smartest factory still needs customers. Nor can a more efficient factory create demand itself. If businesses use better technology mainly to produce more of the same goods, productivity gains could disappear into another round of price competition.
The decisive question is what reaches the consumer. Does improved Chinese manufacturing mean a more reliable appliance, a better car or a genuinely useful product?

One possible future sees China exporting its manufacturing – not the procucts of it – to other countries. Overseas factories could become dependant on on Chinese machinery and technical support. For Chinese businesses, supplying those capabilities could open another route to international growth.
A different kind of Chinese manufacturing power

Could is the operative word there. This technology creates possibilities but it doesn’t guarantee industrial leadership. We can say something with a degree of certainty though, and that’s that China’s position as the world’s manufacturing base is far from over.

No longer reliant on providing cheap labour, China is changing its approach to global production. And by trading manual assembly for artificial intelligence and automation, it ensures its industrial crown remains secure. The Made in China stamp has evolved from a mark of cheap affordability into a baseline for global technological dominance.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/opinions/chinese-manufacturing-dominance/

articles.headline: Can AI Tell Your Fortune? How Chinese Divination Is Going Digital
articles.dek: Career, love, finances, family, health — all of the things you want to ask a fortune teller can now be asked of AI.
articles.summary: Chinese users are feeding birth data into DeepSeek and new apps to read ba zi, feng shui and the I Ching, turning divination into an everyday digital habit, while human masters endure.

cover.alt: A fortune teller at a lantern-lit street stall

blocks.text: By John Lim
Ask an AI chatbot about your career, relationship, or future, and it will probably give you an answer. Ask it to read your ba zi, however, and you enter a very different kind of conversation.

Across Chinese social media, users have been feeding detailed birth information into AI models such as DeepSeek and asking them to interpret their ba zi, or Four Pillars of Destiny. On Xiaohongshu, the practice became a viral trend, with users sharing prompts for everything from relationship compatibility to career and fortune readings. Some users ask whether they should change jobs; others ask about romantic compatibility or when a particular period of good fortune might arrive. In 2025, the trend became prominent enough in China that the hashtag #DeepSeekFortune racked up tens of millions of views on Xiaohongshu.

blocks.alt: RADII offers a deep dive into how tech and AI is being used to update Chinese traditional divination practices like fortune telling.
blocks.caption: Image via Xiaohongshu.

blocks.text: The appeal is obvious. A traditional fortune-teller might require an appointment, a fee, and some idea of what you want to ask. There’s also the potential awkwardness of telling someone your deepest thoughts, most worrying concerns, and other forms of deep desires. An AI oracle is available whenever you are, whether that means after a bad day at work or while wondering if you should text an ex at 1 AM. It can also happily explain the same chart over and over again, without charging by the hour. And, of course, no awkward silence to weather through.

blocks.alt: RADII offers a deep dive into how tech and AI is being used to update Chinese traditional divination practices like fortune telling.
blocks.caption: Image via Caixin Global.

blocks.text: And increasingly, you don’t even need to know what you’re doing. A growing crop of apps now combine AI with ba zi, feng shui, I Ching, Zi Wei Dou Shu and other forms of Chinese metaphysics, turning practices that can take years to learn into something resembling a chatbot conversation.
From Reading the Stars to Reading a Chatbot

Chinese divination encompasses a sprawling collection of traditions rather than one single system. Ba zi, or the Four Pillars of Destiny, uses a person’s year, month, day, and hour of birth to construct a chart based around the traditional Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches. Other systems, such as I Ching divination and Zi Wei Dou Shu, use different methods to interpret a person’s circumstances and possible future.

For generations, accessing these systems often meant finding someone who had spent years learning how to interpret them. That expertise was not simply a matter of plugging information into a formula. A practitioner would interpret a chart, ask questions about a client’s circumstances, and use their experience to decide which details mattered.
AI changes that relationship by putting the interpretation layer into the interface.

blocks.alt: RADII offers a deep dive into how tech and AI is being used to update Chinese traditional divination practices like fortune telling.
blocks.caption: Image via AIBase.

blocks.text: A user can generate a ba zi chart through an app, paste it into ChatGPT, Claude, or DeepSeek, and ask the model to explain it. Some dedicated services now go much further. Cantian AI, for instance, offers ba zi, Liu Yao divination, feng shui and I Ching readings alongside an AI interpretation layer, while YiMatrix combines ba zi with Zi Wei Dou Shu, multiple forms of divination and an AI chat assistant that can explain a user’s chart.

blocks.alt: RADII offers a deep dive into how tech and AI is being used to update Chinese traditional divination practices like fortune telling.
blocks.caption: Image via FengShui AI — 風水大師.

blocks.text: Other apps are making the process even more familiar. FengShui AI offers personalized daily readings, compatibility analysis, I Ching readings, and even the ability to upload photographs of a space for an AI feng shui assessment. Another app, 8Luck.AI, combines ba zi with AI face and palm analysis.
Your Digital Fortune Teller Is Always On
That accessibility may be the most significant change.

A 2025 South China Morning Post report spoke to young Chinese users who were combining traditional astrology apps with generative AI. One 21-year-old user described generating her ba zi chart and then feeding it into ChatGPT to assess her compatibility with her boyfriend.
The questions being asked are remarkably ordinary: Will my career improve? Is this relationship right for me? Should I make this decision? When will things get better?

blocks.alt: RADII offers a deep dive into how tech and AI is being used to update Chinese traditional divination practices like fortune telling.
blocks.caption: Image via Infinity Core.

blocks.text: That may help explain why AI fortune-telling has found an audience among young people who might not necessarily describe themselves as deeply religious or superstitious. A 2026 study of young Chinese users found that people engaged with AI fortune-telling in several ways, including playfully, emotionally, and through combinations of digital tools and existing spiritual practices. Another study of more than 1,000 social-media posts and user interviews found that people often treated LLM fortune-telling less as a precise predictive system and more as a source of emotional support.
In other words, you don’t necessarily have to believe that the chatbot can see your future to find the exercise useful. It can just be curiosity, interest, or even mere amusement.

There is something oddly familiar about this, too. People have long turned to fortune-telling during uncertain periods, whether because they genuinely believe in it or simply want another perspective on a difficult decision, or to find some levity. AI removes much of the friction involved. You don’t have to explain why you’re asking, worry about being judged, or wait for an appointment. You can simply ask again, and again.
What Happens When You Can Ask Fate Until You Like the Answer?

Unlike a human fortune-teller, an AI can produce another reading almost instantly. If the answer doesn’t sound right, you can change the wording of the prompt, provide more information, or ask the question from another angle (for better or worse).

Research into Chinese users of generative-AI fortune-telling has found this behavior precisely. In one 2026 study involving interviews with 22 regular users and an analysis of 1,842 online community posts, researchers found that some users repeated queries until they received interpretations that aligned more closely with what they expected. Users appreciated AI’s convenience and efficiency, but also felt that it lacked some of the spiritual mystique associated with human divination.
That creates an interesting paradox.

Traditional divination is often presented as a way of confronting uncertainty: you ask a question, receive an interpretation, and decide what to do with it. AI can instead turn divination into an iterative conversation. The “oracle” doesn’t necessarily deliver one answer. It gives you an answer, waits for your response, and then gives you another.

blocks.alt: RADII offers a deep dive into how tech and AI is being used to update Chinese traditional divination practices like fortune telling.
blocks.caption: Image via Time Out.

blocks.text: The distinction matters because today’s AI fortune tellers aren’t supernatural machines. Large language models generate responses from patterns in their training data, and specialized applications combine those models with systems for calculating and interpreting traditional charts. Their predictions are not scientifically validated, and even the apps themselves generally frame their readings as guidance, entertainment, or reference rather than certainty.
The New Fortune Teller Doesn’t Need a Crystal Ball

For thousands of years, divination has adapted to whatever tools people had available: calendars, almanacs, coins, charts, stars, and specialized texts. The smartphone may simply be its latest interface.

But as with everything else AI-related, the use cases here are accessibility and immediacy. Someone’s desire to know the future is not dependent on an appointment anymore; they can simply do so through a screen.

blocks.alt: RADII offers a deep dive into how tech and AI is being used to update Chinese traditional divination practices like fortune telling.
blocks.caption: Image via DeepSeek.

blocks.text: Plus, a person who knows nothing about the Four Pillars can now generate a chart in seconds. Someone curious about feng shui can photograph a room and ask for suggestions. Someone worried about a relationship can ask an AI to compare two birth charts. And someone who has never sat across from a fortune-teller can have an extended conversation with one without ever leaving the sofa.

That doesn’t mean the human fortune-teller is about to disappear. Far from it. Traditional practitioners still argue that genuine interpretation requires experience, intuition, and an understanding of the person sitting in front of them. There’s no replacing that.

Instead, divination is becoming less of a specialized service and more of a digital habit. Like trying to figure out how to interview for a job without needing to ask a career coach, or understanding stock exchanges without having to consult a stockbroker.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/how-chinese-divination-is-going-digital

articles.headline: Wallet Wars
articles.dek: Personal agents have arrived, setting off a race for who controls how they spend consumers’ money.
articles.summary: Terry Angelos maps the fight between Stripe’s Link, Shop Pay, PayPal and the card networks over letting AI agents pay for you, and argues open token standards will beat walled gardens.

cover.alt: Rows of stacked dark coins on a wooden surface

blocks.text: By Terry Angelos

Agents such as Instinct, OAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse are bringing personal assistants into text messages and familiar apps. The promise is no longer just better answers; it is getting things done. If my agent can organize my kids’ soccer schedule, it can also order their cleats. If it can plan a trip, it can book the hotel. An assistant that understands my life becomes the starting point for much of my spending.

But completing those tasks requires something intelligence alone cannot provide: permission to pay. If your agent doesn’t have your credit card number, any recommendation from an agent becomes a “to do” list for me. With payment credentials in hand, the agent can complete the task for me.
So, of course, there is a scramble underway for what products and companies are going to help agents pay: enter the Wallet Wars.

Below the waterline, as wallets get connected to agents, there are two battles going on: one is over who can help my agent pay, and the other (more consequential one) is over who lets it transact as me. These seem like the same question but they are not! And the difference between the two is important, both for the user experience of “personal payment flows” (think loyalty programs) and for the economics of payments.
This is not a new challenge

In the early years of the internet, people were skeptical that anyone would ever buy something online. Giving your card number to a website seemed risky and unfamiliar. But online shopping was enough of a draw that people learned to trust the process. If history is a guide, just like last time, people will have no problem trusting agents to make payments on their behalf.

Part of what makes an online payment seem scary is that, to the user, the 16 digit card number represents both the identity of the paying account and the authority to initiate a payment. In reality, we’ve worked for decades on the underlying mechanics to make payments easy, safe, and secure, by effectively separating these two concerns. In the industry we call this “payment tokenization”.

Whenever you trust someone to save your card information (whether it be a merchant, a service, a wallet, or something else), they often also create a payment token. In addition to making the whole process more reliable and trustworthy, they also do nice things like, when your card expires, your Netflix subscription doesn’t have to pause - the actors behind the scenes coordinate, “you’re probably still you”, and keep your shows going. Payment tokenization is the site of many “inside-industry” power struggles for how you pay, that the user never sees - and I won’t inflict those stories on you, but payments professionals are very used to these kinds of standoffs.

Now we have these things called agents, which are a further evolutionary step in separating “the identity of the person / the account that’s going to pay” from “the authority to initiate a payment.” And, while it presents some new and interesting challenges which we’ll go through here, we’re not starting from zero - we’re building on years of precedent of how internet payments already work.
The war to connect

The fastest way to give an agent spending power is to connect a wallet that already holds the consumer’s credentials. Stripe’s Link (300M users), Shopify’s Shop Pay (250M users) and PayPal (400M+ users) bring existing payment relationships to that contest, rather than asking consumers and merchants to start over.

For agent developers, the questions are straightforward: How many of my users already have a payment method stored with you? How many of the merchants support this wallet? Stripe and Shopify have moved quickly, powering payments for Muse and Instinct. But speed of integration is only one advantage. PayPal brings an established network of consumers and businesses. Perhaps agents can give PayPal a second act because the winning wallet needs not the prettiest checkout.
The war for reach

Because no wallet’s checkout button is accepted everywhere, wallets offer alternative paths to reach merchants. For example, Link gives an agent a single-use virtual card to make purchases on behalf of the customer. In this flow, a merchant does not need to integrate Link; instead the agent can present its own virtual card during checkout.

While this expands its merchant acceptance, it doesn’t make the purchase equivalent to using the original card. Instead, two transactions are occurring. One between me and Stripe Link (using my card in the wallet) and one between Stripe Link and the merchant.

This can lead to some sub-optimal experiences. For example, imagine your agent buys something from Walmart. Walmart sees an opportunity to strengthen their customer relationship, and tells you: “We’d love to sign you up for Walmart+!” But if you try to accept their offer, what happens? The whole experience breaks, because the credit cards don’t match.
Stripe is building the AOL of agentic commerce
AOL packaged a messy online world into a curated experience; rather than read the news on an unknown website, AOL fetched the news and brought it to you, inside AOL.

For agentic payments, Stripe is building a similar walled garden where transactions occurring inside Stripe’s ecosystem never need to exchange credentials. If your agent shops at a Stripe merchant, Stripe can already charge the card on file without an agent touching it.

When transacting at non-Stripe merchants, Link has been the most aggressive wallet to use its own virtual cards for payment. This means that Stripe is actually buying the item on-your-behalf, rather than the agent acting as you. The good news is that the transaction succeeds. The bad news is the relationship between you and the merchant has changed and this creates problems outside the AOL-like walls.

Suppose I tell my agent to use my Chase Mileageplus card to book a flight at United. If my Link wallet charges that Mileageplus account, but pays United with a Stripe issued virtual card, the money may move without delivering everything I intended (where are my promised miles?). Link’s own terms warn that underlying card offers, benefits and rewards do not carry through in certain separate-payment-method transactions.
Stripe can reproduce the payment without necessarily preserving the relationship. That is the distinction between payment interoperability and relationship interoperability.
The war for routing
Now imagine my agent can access Link, Shop Pay and PayPal, with several cards available across them.
Which should it use?

I might prefer my airline card for airfare, another card for groceries, or the payment method already saved with a particular merchant. I may prioritize rewards for one purchase and purchase protection for another.

As we use agents going forward, “buy it” is not a complete payment instruction. The agent needs to understand my preferences, the merchant relationship and the consequences of each payment route. And when those interests conflict, whose economics should it optimize, the consumer’s, the merchant’s or the agent platform’s?
We are headed to a world where an agent needs a payment policy, not just a payment credential.
The war for liability

With so many intermediaries between me and my purchase, who bears liability for mistakes? Suppose I authorize my agent to spend $500 on a hotel. It stays within budget but books the wrong dates. The hotel delivers exactly what the agent ordered.
Who gives me my money back?

We are re-writing the rules for liability as each of the participants define their role. For example,- the card networks have frameworks for scoped payment credentials that restrict spending by amount and merchant and preserve the cardholder rights to chargebacks. Most wallets treat transactions from a connected agent as authorized even when the agent misinterprets instructions. The agent too will have to show that it followed the guidance set by the user.

So we have overlapping permissions and recourse. Authorization, correct execution and purchase protection are different problems. Authorization is addressed by payment tokens. Execution by the agent and purchase protection by the wallet and card issuer.
For consumers, the question will be much simpler: when my agent gets it wrong, who makes it right?
The Future is Open Standards

As agents scale, the AOL-era will give way to open standards where agents preserve my relationship with the merchant, use my preferred issued card and ensure my transaction earns the right loyalty and benefits rewards.

The card networks announced a set of standards for Agentic Commerce that allows agents to safely receive my card and (more importantly) transact as me. Each network has its own world salad approach: Visa has Visa Intelligent Commerce, Mastercard has AgentPay and AMEX has ACE.

These standards from the card networks move us from the “AOL of agentic payments” to something more like the open web. The best of all worlds is a future where my agent can use my credit card, without having my credit card. How could we achieve this?
• I store my card in a trusted wallet

• Before a transaction starts, the wallet creates a scoped agentic token that can safely be handed to the agent and given to the merchant. The token can’t be used by another party or merchant and has built-in safeguards that match the prompt (“don’t spend more than $100”)
• The merchant receives the agentic token and can transact using this credential, which maps back to my original card and preserves all loyalty and cardholder benefits.
AOL was a helpful set of training wheels for getting everyone online, but the open web ultimately won. We think the same thing will happen with agents as well.

Le projet repose sur un accord entre l’ETH Zurich et IBM prévu initialement jusqu’en 2029. Il s’inscrit aussi dans un nouveau pôle suisse d’innovation quantique réunissant recherche académique et partenaires industriels.

articles.headline: Anthropic’s numbers, OpenAI at $70bn and Gemini 4
articles.dek: The news section of Benedict’s Newsletter No. 663
articles.summary: Benedict Evans says Anthropic’s leaked 2025 figures matter less than inference economics, sees Gemini 4 back on top with no winner-takes-all, and doubts OpenAI’s new consumer agents.

cover.alt: The New York Stock Exchange building on Wall Street
cover.credit: Photo: Arild Vågen / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.text: Anthropic’s 2025 numbers

Reuters got hold of Anthropic’s S1 IPO filing, originally scheduled for the summer and now apparently targeting November, and published the revenue and profitability for 2025: $4.6bn revenue and an $8bn operating loss. However, the company’s ‘annualised’ monthly gross revenue had grown to $9bn last December and reached $65bn by July: I simply do not care what this company looked like when it was less a 10th of the size. The real questions remain: what is the profitability of inference versus the cost of building the next model today, and how will the cost and profitability of each of those evolve over the next one and three years as the models get bigger and all those trillions of dollars of capex come online? Compared to that, focusing on numbers from before agentic coding is deeply unserious.
OpenAI at $70bn

Illustrating the point, Axios reports that OpenAI is now close to $70bn ‘annualised run-rate’ revenue (this time net revenue, unlike Anthropic's gross number) - these aren’t comparable numbers, but they clearly indicate that Anthropic’s early lead in agentic coding has been sharply eroded.
Gemini 4

This is another big/small story. After a couple of months of radio silence, Google came back and released its new version of Gemini, which puts it straight back at the top of the leaderboards. While Anthropic and OpenAI still set the agenda up to a point, Google, Meta and SpaceX are all in the same bracket, and the Chinese labs really aren’t very far behind. If you are deep, deep, deep in the Valley, then you talk about China or Meta being weeks or months behind, but there are very few consumer or enterprise use cases where you can tell the difference, especially when you’re using a model from six months ago to optimise cost and performance. There’s no sign at the moment of any winner-takes-all effect, nor of any other reason why frontier labs have pricing power that extends beyond a shortage of compute.
OpenAI tries agents again, again

OpenAI tried yet again (I’ve lost count) to make consumer agents work, this time with almost exactly the same cute child-like aesthetic as Meta’s Muse, but proposing lots of different agents called Dots that you can assign different tasks. Watching the launch video exposes a lot of the same underlying problems, though: the use cases that OpenAI proposes are either hard-core technical and deep in their comfort zone, or things that only happen to you very occasionally, like (and I wish I was making this up) using Dots to plan your wedding.

I think the underlying question is that you have the same blank screen problem we’ve had since 2022, the models remain jagged and unpredictable as to what they can really do (and agents add another layer as retailers block them) and I wonder whether the right path is to make these horizontal and ambient so they can watch you and suggest things, or vertical and use-case-specific, embedded inside apps. Of course, that was also the question for search.
Full Spectrum Meta

Meta continues its Muse push with a new SME offering, connecting into all sorts of SaaS products (Dropbox, Figma, Shopify etc). Many of these are building agentic tools of their own, of course: everyone wants to make everyone else into a dumb API call, and no-one really knows the right point of aggregation.

Meanwhile, Meta also revealed more of its plan to run an enterprise cloud: it hired the CEO of MongoDB (he was only there for 11 months) to run a new unit which will offer Meta’s infrastructure plus services built on Muse. As I noted before, this gives Meta a path to more revenue to load onto any infrastructure it builds and then can’t fill while it builds consumer and ad products on top, but building a new enterprise infra business from zero, in an entirely new space at that, is easier said than done - different culture, sales models, incentives, products… (and look at how Google Cloud has struggled).
OpenAI’s fallout continues

Meanwhile, contra the suggestion below that it’s being too careless, OpenAI said it postponed the launch of a new model because it couldn’t guarantee it had the right controls around it, and it apologised to Australia for its models accessing a range of government systems in unauthorised ways. And buried in an updated discussion of its investigation into the Hugging Face incident, it discloses that it has now notified over 100 different organisation that its models accessed their systems in various inappropriate ways. This is a failure of management and engineering, not ‘alignment’, and now has people asking about some pretty substantial legal liability issues.
The week in AI

Nvidia jumped on the cyber flurry of the last few months with a hardware-based platform to enforce sandbox policies and keep models under control. The announcement comes with lots of logos (they always do), but why would a frontier lab let another company own its research and product-build environment like this?

AMD bought Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs, which aims to build physical and causation models beyond LLMs, for $8.2bn in stock. It feels funny to put an $8bn deal in ‘other news’, but that’s 2026. The PPT for this deal writes itself: AMD wants to follow Nvidia up the stack and World Labs is available, while World Labs needs far more ‘free’ compute.
Doordash drones.
Bloomberg points out that Amazon has been quietly giving its drivers smart glasses with cameras for the last year, and predicts a backlash is coming. Meanwhile, training data!
Oura, the smart ring maker, pulled its IPO citing market conditions - there is some discussion of how much the imminent Anthropic and (further out) OpenAI IPOs are crowding out anything else.
Source: Benedict’s Newsletter No. 663 (free edition) — https://www.ben-evans.com/newsletter

articles.headline: Winning the Relay Race: Long-Running Agents in High-Value Customer Journeys
articles.dek: What an AI-native Red Ventures could look like
articles.summary: David Haber says agents that can work for weeks will take over multi-step journeys like legal intake, mortgages and insurance claims, letting vendors get paid for outcomes, not seats.

cover.alt: A hand in a suit sleeve passing a relay baton

blocks.text: By David Haber

Traditionally, calling your internet provider’s support hotline about an outage went something like this. A robotic voice greeted you as a valued customer, then made you spend several minutes on phone menus (“press 3 for technical support, 2 for internet, then 4 for all other issues”). You were put on hold, feeling forgotten, until a service representative finally picked up and asked for your name, account number and issue. If restarting your router didn’t fix the problem, you were put on hold again, only to tell another representative the whole story a second time before receiving a technician appointment.

AI is already transforming support interactions like this one. Instead of grappling with a robotic voice and several service representatives, an AI agent can now pick up right away. It can see your account, check whether other customers in your area are also affected and either resolve simple problems directly or book a technician. No more “all our service representatives are currently busy” and no more hold music. Until recently, this was the technological limit.

But now, new capabilities are allowing agents to follow threads and execute tasks over longer horizons. We believe this will allow AI companies to go beyond individual customer interactions and rethink how to address complex customer journeys that run over weeks and months. AI will guide insurance customers from an initial call to payout, mortgage borrowers from pre-approval to closing, and enterprise leads from their first demo to signature. This will not only create better outcomes for those customers, but also let the AI vendor get paid for the resulting revenue expansion, not just for cost savings.
Value Only Appears At The End Of The Relay Race

There are many kinds of businesses where creating value for customers takes many steps, over weeks and months. Let’s take the traditional plaintiff law case preparation journey as an example. Prospective cases often arrive as leads by phone, where intake specialists gather the key facts and pass them to an attorney who evaluates whether to take on a client. Once a firm signs a case, investigation and evidence collection follow: Paralegals order police reports, try to get in contact with witnesses, and send spoliation letters to defendants to preserve evidence while keeping clients updated on progress. Firms then wait for client medical treatment to conclude before drafting a medical chronology and handing information to attorneys to finalize the demand letter.

This process is what we historically would have called a “relay race”: a long journey with risk of drop-off or value leakage at each handoff. Potential clients usually call several personal injury firms and often sign with the firm that gets back to them the quickest. So cases can drop out of the funnel if clients only reach voicemail or if the qualification decision is slow. Once a client is signed, evidence collection involves many parallel threads at once and firms may not have the persistence to call a potential witness for the fifth time after the previous four attempts went unanswered. In addition, labor constraints can keep firms from reviewing every piece of evidence in detail, especially for seemingly routine, low-value claims. A firm may accept the first offer when a detailed read of the doctor’s note would have surfaced indicators of a brain injury, increasing settlement value. Finally, cases can run for months, require numerous contributors, and involve information distributed across documents, stakeholders, and systems. This makes it nearly impossible to maintain the full picture on every client. As a result, important bills may not be reflected in the demand letter or treatment gaps may remain unexplained, driving lower settlement value.
The Long-Running Agent Opportunity

Until recently, AI agents mostly handled bounded tasks (“Send this follow-up email”, “Summarize that call”, “Create this document”) and narrow interactions. For instance, customer support has been a great early AI use case because the problem space is well-defined, making high reliability achievable, while still allowing for customization based on company-specific policies. Interactions are brief, outcomes are verifiable, and if AI agents encounter edge cases they cannot handle, existing support teams are usually still in place for escalations.

Now, long-running agents are able to pursue goals across dozens of steps, modalities, and longer time horizons, allowing them to take on relay races from start to finish. In the plaintiff law example, a long-running agent could be assigned to a case from the initial intake call with the goal of maximizing the client’s recovery. The agent would save and retrieve context on the case as needed. It wakes based on events or deadlines, proactively dispatches sub-agents to contact witnesses, update the client, and interact with attorneys across phone, email, or text. It then consolidates findings, plans subsequent moves, drafts documents for review, and drives the case towards the best possible outcome. Across clients, it keeps learning, as each case generates data which helps the agent process the next case better than the current one.

The agent addresses key value leaks observed in today’s relay race. At the start of the journey, clients are no longer lost to slow case evaluation as the agent is available regardless of the hour or weekday and can assess cases nearly instantaneously. Evidence collection is no longer bounded by human capacity, as the case agent can spin up an additional sub-agent at any moment to place the fifth, tenth, or even twentieth phone call. As agents are nearly infinitely scalable, even seemingly routine cases get worked fully and each piece of evidence is reviewed in detail, surfacing the potential brain injury that might otherwise have been missed. And finally, the agent keeps a complete record of the case, from witness phone call transcripts to police reports and medical records, making sure no information gets lost.
Getting Paid For Outcomes

Beyond closing these leaks, owning the full customer journey can change the economics for the agent vendor. As agents help deliver outcomes with higher quality at greater speed, they can drive revenue uplift, not just cost reduction for customers. More importantly, as impact is observable and attributable to agents, vendors can participate in the upside they create by pricing based on work products or outcomes. In plaintiff law, for instance, a single case is a discrete unit of work and the value of the resulting outcome, the settlement amount, is clearly identifiable. In addition, outcomes can be linked to agents more easily as they drive a larger share of the final work product. Vendors may then share in topline expansion, reaching contract values previously unattainable by solely focusing on cost reduction.

Admittedly, switching to outcome-based pricing is not frictionless. In plaintiff law, most states prohibit non-lawyers from sharing in legal fees, so pricing would need to align with settlement values without taking a direct share of them. In other verticals, vendors may face objections from procurement teams who do not yet have precedents for outcome-based contracts. And even though agents move closer to fully owning outcomes, attribution debates will likely surface initially. Successfully deploying long-running agents will therefore be a commercial challenge as much as a technical one.
Still, getting paid for outcomes on high-value customer journeys is not a new idea.
The Case For An AI-native Red Ventures

Red Ventures (RV) is a great historical example. RV was founded by Ric Elias and Dan Feldstein and pioneered digital end-to-end outsourced sales operations for long-term consumer contracts. As an example, for insurance policies, RV would collect details on customers when they were searching for these products (by owning sites like homeinsurance.com), reach out, walk them through coverage options, and close the policy. By fully owning this journey, RV collected a payment from the insurer for each policy it closed. This used to work extremely well: according to S&P Global, RV generated ~$370M in EBITDA on ~$1.4B in sales in 2022.

Now, this model seems structurally under threat. At the top of the funnel, consumers are changing how they discover products. Instead of relying on Google search or comparison sites to explore and compare products, they can now ask a personal agent like Meta’s Muse or Instinct for product recommendations directly, lowering the value of owning traditional exploration sites. Further downstream, instead of hundreds of humans running linear funnels, long-running agents can work across far more complex journeys. They will do so across products, and communication modalities, in parallel, in any language and at scale, with infinite persistence. RV’s EBITDA decline to an estimated ~$160M in 2025, driven by customer churn and softer ad spend, provides an early indication of the model’s vulnerability as AI will transform the industry further going forward.
Three Ways To Market
There are different ways to bring long-running agents to market.

(1) Selling the Platform: Under this motion, the vendor sells the long-running agent as software, supporting the enterprise in its existing operations. The plaintiff law case agent integrating with an existing team and their workflows is a good example. Selling a platform allows for revenue upside as there are often no comparable software or outsourced services contracts in place anchoring prices. This, however, also extends sales cycles as new budget lines need to be created, and it is harder to clearly attribute outcomes to an agent that interfaces with several departments across the enterprise.

(2) Selling the Service: Here, the vendor takes over an already outsourced service to deliver a desired outcome more effectively, just like Red Ventures owning the entire customer acquisition journey for an insurance carrier. This approach shortens sales cycles as the ROI math for buyers is simple and budget lines for BPOs already exist. However, existing, pre-AI pricing models may not reflect the true value the long-running agent can deliver and many high-value journeys are run in-house today, limiting the reach of this approach.

(3) Going Full-Stack: A full-stack approach means vertically integrating and becoming an AI-native player. For instance, instead of selling a long-running agent to a debt collection firm, you could buy debt portfolios and collect them yourself, allowing you to fully capture any AI upside created and address attribution problems. However, this also means owning parts of the service like licensing or compliance, which are outside the actual customer journey, adding distractions and operational complexity.

It is too early to tell which of these approaches will prevail, but we are convinced that long-running agents will win the relay race at scale and expand the market addressable by AI from a share of labor budgets to a share of revenue. Plaintiff case preparation is only one example and we expect to see agents drive outcomes across other high-value journeys like mortgage origination, insurance claims processing, complex enterprise sales and countless others. If you are working on capturing this opportunity, we would love to hear from you!
Source: a16z — https://www.a16z.news/p/winning-the-relay-race-long-running

articles.headline: How is NikeSKIMS differentiating at its China launch?
articles.dek: NikeSKIMS has opened its first China store as the premium activewear market gets crowded.
articles.summary: NikeSKIMS opened in Shanghai with Kim Kardashian, XXS–4X sizing and in-store alterations, betting that fit can set it apart from Alo and Lululemon while Nike’s China sales slump.

cover.alt: Kim Kardashian posing with two guests at the NikeSKIMS launch in Shanghai
cover.credit: Image: NIKE via Rednote / DAO Insights

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• NikeSKIMS combines Nike’s performance technology with SKIMS’ sculpting design to distinguish itself in China’s competitive premium activewear market
• Its Shanghai store makes fit central to the experience, offering XXS–4X sizing and alterations for selected products
• Kardashian’s appearance generated launch attention, but the temporary space’s longer-term value will depend on customer experience and repeat purchases

Chinese social feeds are brimming with Kim K content this week as the star hits Shanghai for the China launch of NikeSKIMS. That’s her collaboration brand with the sportswear giant. It’s been successful in the States. Now it’s looking for a slice of the China market.

The trouble is this market is a tough one. Premium activewear in China is dominated by a fierce competitor in Lululemon. A slew of new entrants are also looking to compete, including Alo, which plans to open eight new stores over the next few years and have seen stunning sales figures in the opening minutes of their Tmall launch. So, what is NikeSKIMS doing to stand out?
‘Designed to sculpt, engineered to perform’

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NikeSKIMS｜共塑力与美_3_NIKE_来自小红书网页版.jpg

blocks.text: The brand’s key differentiator is the promise of Nike performance and SKIMS’ body-focussed design. Essentially, the clothes are designed to help you look good while you move.
There are specific product foundations behind that message. In its original global collection, the Matte range combined smoothing and sculpting with Nike’s sweat-wicking Dri-FIT technology.

The Shanghai launch spans nine fabric collections, footwear and accessories. Against Alo’s Californian wellness positioning, NikeSKIMS’ product range places greater emphasis on how clothes shape and support the body.
Embedding the message into a store experience

The store needs to sell that message. It does it by ensuring the clothing fits all body types. Sizes range from XXS to 4X. Alterations are available on selected products. Lounge areas are also present to support the shopping experience.

This is an interesting point to note. Alo’s new sanctuary stores include lounge areas, though theirs seem to go further, adding cafes and work-out spaces. The idea is one that Lululemon used extensively: selling premium activewear through community. At the new NikeSKIMS store, the space is geared primarily toward clothing.
Kim K attention

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NikeSKIMS｜与Kim相见上海🤎_3_NIKE_来自小红书网页版.jpg

blocks.text: While NikeSKIMS’ original global campaign featured pro athletes from Serena Williams to Sha’Carri Richardson, China’s splash also focusses on Kim Kardashian. She was there a day before the opening, joined by Kris Jenner and Khloé Kardashian, alongside guests including basketball player Li Meng and swimmer Stephanie Au.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NikeSKIMS｜与Kim相见上海🤎_5_NIKE_来自小红书网页版.jpg

blocks.text: These associations will speak to women interested in both exercise and appearance. But celebrity openings are familiar territory in this market. At Alo’s nearby store launch a few days later were three big names, including Zhao Lusi (赵露思), their global brand ambassador.
Five months to make an impression

The Shanghai space will only operate until February 2027. Planned product experiences, try-ons and community activities are in place to give NikeSKIMS a route into longer-term consumer relationships, and a more permanent store footprint in China.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/上海Nike✖️skims排队真的很夸张_1_-AP_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Image: Rednote user/-AP

blocks.text: The short lease is likely a strategy of not overcommitting. The temporary format also offers useful feedback on products, sizing and service before further expansion. But for all its caution Nike, in its role as parent brand, does have something big at stake in this joint brand taking off.
A new proposition during Nike’s China reset

Nike is in troubled waters in China at the moment. Its Greater China sales fell 26% in its fiscal quarter ending August 2026. And that’s a problem that’s been persisting for a while. NikeSKIMS gives Nike an additional proposition for the market amid a wider global rollout.
The Dao view: Can the fit promise outlast the launch?
NikeSKIMS has connected its positioning to tangible details: sculpting fabrics, extended sizing and selected alterations. That gives customers something concrete to assess against the competition.

But will that generate repeat purchases? Community activities are there to sustain engagement beyond the launch. The difference between what NikeSKIMS can offer, and what Alo or Lululemon can bring to the table will be the decider. With the launch over and the propositions laid plan, the market will be won by the product works better in everyday use.

articles.headline: Loss of Cell Identity Drives Human Aging
articles.dek: That’s what biological (epigenetic) aging clocks are measuring
articles.summary: Eric Topol explains new Nature and Cell papers suggesting we age as cells lose their epigenetic identity and drift into a fibrous, inflammatory state that might be reversible.

cover.alt: Red-stained actin filaments of cardiac fibroblasts under a microscope

blocks.text: By Eric Topol

Two new papers, one published today in Nature by Vadim Gladyshev and colleagues at Harvard, and a recent one in Cell by Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte and his team at Altos Labs, have provided a new model for the biology of aging, and what might be done to reverse it. Until recently we accepted that aging of cells was due to “wear and tear” like rusting out a car. The idea that accumulated damage is the principal pathway for cell aging is now complemented by the loss of cell identity model. We don’t know the relative contribution or interdependence of these 2 models in the aging process.

blocks.caption: Two different models for why cells age, made with ChatGPT

blocks.text: In this edition of Ground Truths I’m going to explain the loss of cell identity, how it leads to mesenchymal drift (fibrous scarring and inflammation), and how this new model furthers the potential to intervene in the aging process.
Establishing and Maintaining Cellular Identity

In embryonic and early development, our cells establish an identity. It’s locked in throughout our lives, except when it’s lost during the aging process. Although the DNA of every cell of our body is the same (or very close, if interested, see), the epigenetic structure, that includes methylation side chains, histones, nucleosomes and chromatin, is 3-dimensional and differs as a function of cell type. This is happening in the cell’s “mission control,” the nucleus. The epigenetic structure is the bedrock for our cell-specific identity.

There’s a 3-tier regulatory “grammar” that maintains the cell identity as shown below.(Figure from the Nature paper). The fast layer responds to acute stress in a matter of minutes to hours and relies on production of transcription factors, like AP-1. The intermediate layer takes days to weeks to respond, going through cell state transitions such as activating a cell to promote healing and return to its basal state. The key is the slow layer, he one that locks and insulates the cell identity, the hard boundary, relying on chromatin architecture.
Loss of Identity and Mesenchymal Drift

That gets us to Waddington’s epigenetic landscape model for how cells differentiate or de-differentiate, a model that has held up well from Conrad Waddington in 1957! A cell sitting down in the valley (Figure below, culled together from the Nature paper) represents a distinct specialized cell. The deep slope indicates the robustness, also called canalization, accompanied by a deep basin, maintains the identity of the cell, promotes its stability. The differentiated cell is “staying in its lane” in the landscape model and is constrained from sliding out, shifting identity. But with aging, the valleys lose their slope, the basin becomes shallow, there is loss of epigenetic constraints, and there is instability of cell identity. That sets up drift of cell identity, or what can be regarded as mesenchymal drift.

Over the lifespan, as shown on the right side of the Figure below, after peak maturation with the specialized cells (brain, liver heart,kidney, etc) fully and irrevocably differentiated (peak functional state below), the valleys are losing slope and the basins are progressively getting shallower, known as decanalization. The problem is that there is no evolutionary pressure to keep the grooves, valleys and basin in their youthful state, because the “selection shadow” is a post-reproductive trajectory.

The polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) can be seen as the sculptor of this epigenetic landscape, the molecular machinery that shapes the grooves, valleys, and basin. It establishes the hard boundary, the deep epigenetic constraints for cell identity.

Epigenetic clocks are remarkably informative across 348 mammalian species, including humans, for predicting maximal lifespan and life history, but we didn’t know what they are actually measuring. It turns out it’s PRC2, the pace of slow layer erosion! (Figure below, to be precise, it’s the PRC2 low-methylated regions).

PRC2 comes into play when there is chronic inflammation overriding the fast layer capacity to respond and blocking PRC2, leading to erosion of the Waddington landscape, promoting cell identity loss. Even after chronic inflammation is resolved, there are epigenetic changes in chromatin that can persist. This loss of epigenetic grammar can also be the foundation for cancer cells. Eventual erosion of the slow layer essentially portends architectural collapse of the Waddington landscape.

blocks.caption: Schematic of PRC2, what epigenetic clocks are capturing. Made with Google Notebook

blocks.text: The mesenchymal state, as schematically shown below, in this example for an epithelial cell representative of all differentiated, specialized cells.

blocks.caption: Schematic of drift, made with Google Notebook

blocks.text: Now we turn to the Cell paper which goes deep on the mesenchymal drift. This denotes the change of cells to a mesenchymal state, resembling fibroblasts, engendering fibrous scar, laying down extracellular matrix, like mushy putty. It has been verified in 46 tissue types and is part and parcel of disease progression and poor outcomes, as shown below (Figure from the Cell paper). If you are checking for the tie-in between mesenchymal drift and age-related diseases, you’ll find them here, from atherosclerosis, to age-related macular degeneration, to Alzheimer’s disease.
Interventions to Maintain or Restore Identity

Now that we have an enhanced understanding of the process, which has a positive feedback loop as depicted below, fibroblast sthat are activating in turn activating more fibroblasts to induce scarring (Figure from the Cell paper), how can we intervene to freeze the drift, avoid the slow layer erosion, and preserve the Waddington landscape, keeping cells locked in their designated identity? Or, even more ambitious, actually turn back the loss of erosion that has occurred?

Caloric restriction (CR), with its attendant reduced acetyl CoA, and reduced PRC2 methylation, promotes the preservation of slow layer architecture, conceptually freezing the drift. CR has been shown to promote lifespan in mammalian species but the results in non-human primates have been inconsistent, and the magnitude and duration of caloric restriction likely required in people is impractical. Still there may be, theoretically, a partial effect of avoidance of high caloric intake to help prevent erosion.

The use of the Yamanaka stem cell factors is the far-reaching intervention—rejuvenating cells— that has attracted the most attention and huge investment by biotech companies. But it’s tricky because it requires a brief exposure to the 4 transcription factors, OSKM (Oct-4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc), called “partial” epigenetic reprogramming, in order to avoid full reprogramming, which erases their memory and turns cells into pluripotent stem cells. That carries an increased risk for cancer. But partial reprogramming using short bursts, rejuvenation is seen, with restoration of cell identity in aged human fibroblasts (even from age 96 years) and in animal models. The slow layer is restored, the PRC2 domains are re-established, and the mesenchymal drift is actively reversed. An alternative to short exposure for partial reprogramming is the use of 3 transcription factors OSK (no c-Myc) which is being tested in a pilot study of patients with severe optic nerve damage using direct eye injection.

The Nature paper also gets into lithium as an intervention for maintaining neuron identity by interfering with the pathway of slow layer failure. I won’t get into the details of all the mediators (β-catenin, EDH2-USP7, KDM1A, REST, GSK3β, etc) but lithium’s impact on GSK3β blocks tau phosphorylation in experimental models. Lithium orotate has been raised as a candidate for preventing Alzheimer’s, as I’ve previously written about, and this mechanism may be operative.
Closing Comments

There continues to be extraordinary progress in the science of aging. Beyond the old dogma that this is just the cumulative outgrowth of cell mutations and damage, we now understand the epigenetic basis: the loss of cell identity serves as both a driver and result of the aging process. The basic 3-tiered grammar is understood, as are the potential interventions to freeze the mesenchymal drift or directly restore (“rejuvenate”) cell identity. Whether the latter will be capable of safely bringing back the Waddington landscape and reverse aging in humans at the wheel body, organ, or tissue level, remains uncertain.

But we know that chronically stressing the fast layer can be detrimental for the integrity of the essential slow layer. It follows that lifestyle factors, like a pro-inflammatory diet, lack of exercise, or poor sleep quality, can be viewed as chronic stressors that could promote the slow layer erosion and accelerate the loss of cell identity.

The mesenchymal drift story, a fibroblast-like takeover due to loss of cell identity, is exceedingly important as an explanation for the incidence and progression of so many diseases. Slippage of identity can lay the foundation for a cell to become cancerous, yet another bad sequelae. Undoubtedly, loss of cell identity is a major underpinning of age-related diseases.

I was frankly surprised that the new Nature paper did not cite the prior Cell one, since the refined model had much of its basis previously described. Perhaps that was a simple oversight. If there is more interest in partial epigenetic reprogramming, I recommend 2 prior papers (here and here).

One practical takeaway from this work is finally knowing what the epigenetic clock is measuring. I interviewed Steven Horvath, the pioneer of epigenetic clocks when, not very long ago, it was unclear what information was being captured and how these clocks were so accurate. Now it is.

I have purposely omitted many details in this post to not lose the reader. That oversimplification may be disturbing to the epigeneticists. On the other hand, others will say this was above their head. It’s always hard to strike the right balance, especially for a complex topic like this, but I hope you found it helpful. If we are going to slow our aging process and extend our healthspan, understanding the biology will be essential.

NB. I wrote this post. No AI. I did use AI to generate three of the Figures as noted above to help the reader visualize what I was writing about. I have no conflicts of interest related to this topic or post.
