articles.headline: The $108 Billion AI Opportunity for Specialty Practices
articles.dek: Four ways AI can help practices reach more patients and get paid for the care they deliver
articles.summary: A Prosper AI study published by a16z estimates AI could add about $125,000 a year per specialist by answering calls, rebooking patients, preventing denials and collecting bills.

cover.alt: A doctor listening to a patient’s back with a stethoscope

blocks.text: By Xavier de Gracia
Across the United States, specialty medical practices are under growing financial pressure. The cost of running a practice is rising faster than revenue.

While the discussion around AI in healthcare has mostly focused on its potential to lower costs and increase efficiency, AI can have a meaningful impact on the other side of the ledger: revenue. Prosper AI conducted a study to quantify the revenue opportunity tied to where practices can introduce AI to provide more consistent, reliable care and improve practice economics in the process.

Prosper AI leveraged data from interactions across patients and insurance companies accounting for more than $3 billion in care managed, and combined that data set with specialty-specific data from the Medical Group Management Association (MGMA). Prosper AI then conducted original research, a phone-access study called CallIQ, to assess the current state of patient access, covering approximately 2,000 practices across 29 states; the specialties included dermatology, ophthalmology, gastroenterology, OB-GYN, primary care, and orthopedics.

blocks.caption: Data on total gap and contributions for each of four levers; Revenue gaps per physician

blocks.text: Key Findings
Our research identifies four actionable levers within practice leaders’ control, representing an estimated annual revenue opportunity of approximately $125,000 per physician.

1. CAPTURE DEMAND: Convert missed calls to appointments. Even during office hours, 1 in 6 calls go unanswered. Using AI to answer calls and optimize how schedules are filled can generate an average of $44,800 per physician in annual revenue.

2. RECAPTURE DEMAND: Re-engage existing patients. Only 54 percent of patients due for a follow-up visit return on schedule; 40 percent come back late and 6 percent never return. Proactive outreach with the help of AI to bring these patients back sooner can unlock up to $37,400 in additional revenue per physician.

3. PROTECT REIMBURSEMENTS: Prevent avoidable denials. Front-end errors, such as billing an inactive insurance plan, skipping a required insurer approval, or misspelling a patient’s name, drive nearly half of claim denials. Accurate benefits checks done using AI in advance of a visit can eliminate avoidable denials and translate into an average of $28,500 a year per physician.

4. RECOVER REVENUE: Recover the patient responsibility. Patients now pay 36 percent of the cost of their care, and nearly 8 percent of what they owe goes unpaid. Outbound AI calls to patients to recover the amount they are responsible for, for care that has been provided, adds up to $14,100 annually per physician.
The Growing Operational Squeeze in Specialty Practices

Specialty practices face compounding margin squeeze as rising costs collide with stagnant reimbursements and severe administrative overhead. Heading into 2027, this squeeze is likely to intensify as inflation persists. Meanwhile, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced that it has no plans to renew a temporary 2.5 percent boost in Medicare reimbursements set to expire at the end of 2026. The expiration of these temporary payment cuts will cascade across specialty practices and add additional pressure on practices. Crucially, these Medicare cuts impact all insurance reimbursements, as commercial health plans benchmark their contract rates directly against Medicare fee schedules. These cuts come at a tough time for practice leaders; 84 percent of medical groups report higher operating costs than a year ago, with an average increase of 11 percent. Meanwhile, inflation-adjusted Medicare physician payments have declined 33 percent since 2001.
The $125,000/Physician Revenue Opportunity
CAPTURE DEMAND: Convert missed calls to appointments

As basic as it sounds, reaching a provider’s office by phone remains a fundamental breakdown in patient access. Prosper’s proprietary CallIQ data analyzing 2,000 practices reveals an 18 percent daytime missed-call rate, with answered callers facing an average wait of 1.5 minutes, and 20 percent stranded on hold for over 5 minutes. After hours, the missed-call rate rises to 81 percent.

Every missed call – and long wait time – creates the possibility of a lost patient or unfilled appointment slot. This adds to a growing problem. Our data shows that 19 percent of provider schedules go unfilled across practices; at some individual practices, as much as half of available capacity remains unused.

The impact of calls that go unanswered can extend beyond a single lost appointment. Poor phone responsiveness can create a negative patient experience that affects reviews, referrals, and the likelihood that patients that need care come back for it. AI-enabled patient communication delivers 24/7 coverage, enabling practices to handle more inquiries, convert higher call volumes, and maximize provider capacity. When scheduling is fast and frictionless, patient behavior shifts — elevating provider appeal and actively driving patient acquisition. Practices that are easy to reach and schedule actively grow practice volume by attracting patients looking for accessible care.

At Piedmont Plastic Surgery and Dermatology in North Carolina, with Prosper AI handling its calls, the practice saw a 17 percent lift in appointments booked in August 2026, compared to August the year prior. Across their 37 providers, appointments booked rose from 19,209 in August 2025 to 22,524 in August 2026.

Wait times during peak hours fell from seven minutes to zero, and the practice was able to serve 50 callers simultaneously, up from 15 the year prior. Based on an MGMA benchmark of $392 on average for a dermatology visit, the additional 3,315 appointments booked would translate to an estimated $1.3 Million in revenue for that month alone.
RECAPTURE DEMAND: Re-engage existing patients

One of the least visible sources of lost revenue is patients who simply fall out of the care cycle. A patient may be told to return in six months, schedule an annual skin check, come back after surgery, or return for ongoing management of a chronic condition. Unless the next appointment is booked before the patient leaves or the practice has an effective recall system, some of those visits never happen. Unlike a no-show, which creates a visible opening in the schedule, an unscheduled follow-up may never register as lost revenue at all. Missed appointments that are never rescheduled create a similar problem. Across medical specialties, the average no-show rate reaches 18.8 percent with gastroenterology being the highest, at 25.7 percent.

A Massachusetts General Hospital study found that nearly 19 percent of dermatology appointments were missed, and only 41 percent of those patients returned to the practice within the following year. Cost concerns are a key factor contributing to missed care. The problem is also growing, likely due to patients’ sensitivity to rising cost: 32 percent of medical practices reported more no-shows in 2026 than in 2025, while just 10 percent reported fewer, amid mounting affordability pressures on patients. AI-enabled recall and 2-way SMS outreach systems can systematically identify patients who are due for follow-up and engage them to schedule, reducing the number who fall out of the care cycle.
PROTECT REIMBURSEMENTS: Prevent avoidable denials

Ensuring full reimbursement starts long before claims are submitted. For practices operating with increasingly tight margins, financial performance depends on accurate, pre-visit insurance eligibility and benefit verification. Prosper AI’s research reveals that practices see an average of 10 percent of their first-submission claims denied. Denial rates for more complex care, such as orthopedics and gastroenterology, are higher at 22 and 16 percent respectively. Every denial creates additional work for staff while delaying, reducing, or potentially eliminating the probability of successful reimbursement.

The sheer volume of denials and appeals has become a major operational burden. Eighty-four percent of healthcare finance professionals describe managing them as a significant challenge, including 35 percent who call it their “biggest challenge” and another 49 percent who describe it as “very challenging.” For practices already struggling with staffing, the problem can become self-reinforcing: Fewer employees are available to ensure claims are accurate before submission or to pursue reimbursement after a denial.

A meaningful share of this leakage is preventable. Missing or inaccurate claim information, incomplete patient registration data, and coding errors are among the leading causes of denials. In ACA Marketplace plans, for example, administrative errors or omissions account for roughly one-quarter of in-network claim denials.

AI-enabled, pre-visit benefit checks can automatically verify coverage details, confirm authorization status, and flag missing patient details before the visit occurs, eliminating simple administrative errors and stopping preventable denials at the source. At a time when practices have limited control over reimbursement rates, capturing more of the revenue they have already earned is one of the financial levers they can directly influence.
RECOVER REVENUE: Recover the patient responsibility

As patients shoulder a larger share of healthcare costs, recovering the amount that patients are responsible for has become increasingly important to ensuring practices can continue to provide quality care. Patient balances include deductibles, coinsurance, copays, and self-pay bills. According to our internal data from completing over five million calls across providers and payers, patients pay an average of 36 percent of the cost of their care across specialty practices. At dermatology practices, patients are responsible for a majority of the costs, at 55 percent.

Yet most patient responsibility is not taken when care is delivered. Medical practices recover an average of just 39 percent of patient-due balances at the time of service, leaving the majority to be recovered afterward. This creates additional administrative work and increases the likelihood that balances will go unpaid. The challenge is growing. In a 2025 survey, 29 percent of medical practices said recovering outstanding patient balances had become more difficult over the previous year, compared with 26 percent that reported improvement.

At one multi-location dermatology practice, AI reminder calls helped recover 48 percent more outstanding patient balances than standard follow-up. In a randomized comparison, households whose balances had reached a third billing statement received either AI calls or the practice’s usual statements and follow-up.

The AI calls explained balances, answered questions about charges and insurance, and offered payment links, payment plans, or a transfer to the billing team. Over approximately 50 days after the third statement, the practice recovered 31.2 percent of outstanding balances in the AI group, compared with 21.1 percent in the standard-follow-up group.
Calculate Your Practice’s Revenue Opportunity
Practice leaders can determine how much revenue they can add through a 2-step process:

1. Identify your specialty’s annual impact per physician. Locate your medical specialty to see the estimated per-physician revenue opportunity across the four levers (convert calls to appointments, re-engage existing patients, avoid preventable denials, recover the patient responsibility).

2. Calculate your total annual opportunity. Take the total per physician for your specialty, and multiply that by the number of full-time physicians in your practice for your total annual revenue opportunity.
The New Frontier: Putting Revenue-Guaranteed Appointments into Practice
Macroeconomics are out of practice leaders’ hands. These four levers are not.

By using AI to convert calls to appointments, re-engage existing patients, avoid preventable denials, and recover the patient responsibility, specialty practices can capture an estimated $125,000 in additional annual revenue per physician. The bigger opportunity is what happens when the four levers work together. That starts with a benefit-verified appointment: an AI-enabled system confirms the patient’s coverage, calculates what the patient will owe, and tells them before the visit. The result isn’t just a fuller schedule. It’s a schedule filled with revenue the practice can count on, because every booked visit has already been checked against how it will be paid. Each step also strengthens another lever. Accurately verified benefits prevent denials. Patients who know their costs upfront are more likely to show up and then pay for the care provided after the visit. And as patients shoulder more of their care costs, a practice that is easy to book and clear about costs stands out, which brings in new patients and starts the cycle again.
Methodology
The CallIQ Study

To measure the current state of patient access, Prosper AI created the CallIQ phone access study. Prosper AI attempted to reach 2,000 practices across 29 states and 6 specialty types: dermatology, ophthalmology, gastroenterology, OB-GYN, primary care, and orthopedics. No appointments were booked. For every call, we tracked two things: the time it took for a live person to answer, and how long it took to begin scheduling.
Public and industry benchmarks
• MGMA reports: revenue, visits and revenue per visit by specialty, which give each practice’s baseline. MGMA DataDive Financials and Operations. Used with permission from MGMA.
• Federal health data (CMS, AHRQ, CDC): visit patterns, how often patients return, time since last check-up, and payer mix
• Peer-reviewed studies: follow-up adherence, claim denials and patient responsibility. These fill gaps where no national dataset exists
Source: a16z — https://www.a16z.news/p/the-108-billion-ai-opportunity-for

articles.headline: Meet the Beijing Kid Who is Rewiring Nike’s Air Max
articles.dek: From notebook sketches to Nike’s Air Works program, Marc Su imagines an Air Max built for creators.
articles.summary: Beijing designer Marc Su, who once faked being sick to enter a Nike contest, created the 3D-printed Air Max Link for Nike’s Air Works program: a sneaker built for others to customise.

cover.alt: Designer Marc Su standing in a brown jacket and sunglasses
cover.credit: Image via Nike Sportswear Beijing / RADII

blocks.text: Marc Su started drawing sneakers before he knew they could become a career.

At 17, the Beijing native was filling school notebooks with sketches of shoes. When Nike launched the first edition of its On Air design competition in 2018, Su was so determined to participate that he once pretended to be sick to make it happen. He submitted an Air Max 95 concept inspired by Shanghai’s maglev train—and somewhere along the way, a teenage obsession became a career plan.

blocks.caption: Marc Su’s concept sketches of what would become the Nike Air Max Link.

blocks.text: Eight years later, Su is back with Nike, this time helping imagine the future of one of the brand’s most recognizable franchises.

His new Air Max Link is the Beijing contribution to Nike Sportswear’s inaugural Air Works program, which brought eight independent designers from cities including London, Los Angeles, Mumbai, New York, Paris, Shanghai, and Tokyo to Nike’s headquarters in Beaverton, Oregon. Working alongside Nike mentors and 3D-footwear company Zellerfeld, the designers were tasked with imagining new expressions of Air Max using 3D printing.
Su’s answer is less a conventional sneaker collaboration than a proposal for what a sneaker could become.

The Air Max Link reworks the visual language of the Air Max 90—itself a landmark of late-’80s and’90s sneaker culture—through the lens of Beijing. Its gray body references the city’s ubiquitous gray-brick architecture, while a fluorescent green Air unit nods to Su’s childhood memory of owning a Volt-colored Air Max 360.
But the real idea is built into the shoe.

The Air Max Link features modular “Link Nail” attachment points inspired by sunmao (榫卯), the centuries-old Chinese mortise-and-tenon construction technique that joins materials through precisely engineered interlocking pieces. The idea is simple: instead of treating a sneaker as a finished object, let the wearer keep designing it.
Attach a team logo. Add a bow. Build a strap. Print something completely ridiculous. The point is that the shoe doesn’t have to stop evolving when it leaves the factory.
“I hope to let every sneaker enthusiast transform from a consumer into a creator,” Su explains.

That philosophy is rooted in Su’s long-running obsession with 3D printing. He first encountered the technology in 2018 while working on design projects and bought his own printer while studying product and furniture design at University of the Arts London. Today, he uses 3D printing for everything from prototypes and furniture components to bicycle parts and computer cases.

For Su, its significance goes beyond making cool-looking objects. He calls 3D printing a form of “technology equality”—comparable, in his view, to the internet’s role in democratizing access to information.

“In the past, you might have needed a large professional factory, or a highly skilled shoemaker, to bring your design to life,” he says. “Now, with 3D printing, I believe the era of ‘everyone is a sneaker designer’ will arrive soon.”

But getting the Air Max Link there was anything but instant. Before heading to Nike’s Oregon headquarters, Su worked through more than 20 design iterations and five full-scale prototypes. Some of his wildest ideas simply couldn’t survive contact with production. The final shoe became a compromise in the best sense—Su’s design language meeting Nike’s engineering capabilities.

That process continued at Nike, where Su worked with his mentor, Nike Running design director Rolando Hernandez, as well as 3D engineers and veteran Air Max designers including Sergio Lozano, who designed the Air Max 95, and Christian Tresser, designer of the Air Max 97.

The result is also a significant technical experiment. The Air Max Link is the first Air Max design to feature an Air unit only in the forefoot, made possible in part by the ability of 3D printing to precisely tune the density of the shoe’s internal structure. Nike’s Air Works project uses FDM 3D printing and Aero TPU to create the shoe body as a single piece, with the Air unit inserted afterward.
For Su, however, the technology only matters if it unlocks something culturally meaningful.

That connection runs deep in Beijing, a city whose sneaker culture was already taking shape during the’90s. Take Yaxin Sports, for example, which was founded in 1990 and became the city’s beacon for sneakerheads. Anyone in the scene will know it as the destination for collectors and limited-edition releases that would go on to inspire the rest of the country’s sneakerhead landscape.

Su belongs to a younger generation growing up with that history already embedded in the city, but also with access to radically different tools. His interests stretch across cycling, underground music, nightlife, product design, and 3D printing, all of which feed into his creative practice.

Nike first tapped into that energy earlier this year during Air Max Day, when Su helped organize Beijing’s “Ghost Market.” More than 50 3D printers were installed at the event, where visitors could design sneaker components, have them scanned and printed, and attach them to shoes. More than 150 creations emerged over four days.
That experience gave Su the central idea for Air Max Link: Beijing’s future sneaker culture shouldn’t be represented by one designer alone.
It should be a platform for the city’s many young creators.

blocks.caption: Scenes from Nike Sportswear Beijing’s unveiling of Su’s Air Max Link sneaker.

blocks.text: That makes the project feel particularly timely. Air Max has spent decades oscillating between technological innovation and nostalgia, with its archive becoming almost as important as its future. Even Nike has acknowledged the challenge of moving the franchise forward while avoiding a constant loop of retros and callbacks.
Marc Su wants to break that loop.
“Air Works’ purpose isn’t to respond to the past, but to look toward the future,” he says. “If we stop moving forward, there will eventually be no ‘past’ left to retro.”

The Air Max Link is therefore not just another futuristic sneaker. It’s a bet on participation—on the idea that the next iconic shoe might not be designed entirely by Nike, or even entirely by a designer.
Maybe it starts with some kid in Beijing drawing sneakers in the margins of a notebook.
All images via Nike Sportswear Beijing.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/meet-the-beijing-kid-who-is-rewiring-nikes-air-max

articles.headline: Liquid Lore: better-for-you drinks are selling feelings over function
articles.dek: Fitt Insider Issue No. 433
articles.summary: Fitt Insider finds Gen Z and millennials buy functional drinks for mood, nostalgia and identity, as brands like hiyo, Cadence and Ghia build worlds around concerts and childhood memories.

cover.alt: Cans of Athletic Brewing non-alcoholic beer on a store shelf

blocks.text: Better-for-you beverages are selling feelings over function.
Using CPG to express themselves, younger gens want drinks with strong personalities.
Joy Juice
Roughly 80% of Gen Z and 75% of millennials drink functional beverages, but they’re not buying based on marketing callouts (i.e., low-sugar); they’re buying into worlds.
Craving both health and joy, Gen Z/A are twice as likely as older cohorts to seek nostalgic sips, and 63% want products that feel “entertaining or inspiring.”
Curating weekly rotations, they’re buying occasion-specific, mood-boosting drinks, sending “Emotional Support Beverage” social media posts up 140% in the past year.
Set and Setting
With trends superseding loyalty, brands are showing up for core memories, appealing to emotion to amplify effects.

Landing $20.8M from alcohol giant Constellation Brands and entertainment company Live Nation, NA social tonic hiyo will double down on music venues and enter Tao Group Hospitality locations to mark “the nights you want to remember.”

Building the playbook, Liquid Death, OLIPOP, poppi, and Athletic Brewing are becoming staples at concerts and sporting events, helping the latter secure >50% NA craft beer market share. Notably, all sell fun over restriction or fear-mongering.
Newstalgia
Believing performance should “taste like a memory” not “feel like punishment,” Cadence adds electrolytes to flavors like cola and orange soda “from the cookout.”

Arguing next-gen luxury is about how/where brands show up, not just high prices, it’s calling out the sameness of ads showing “just a pretty person running” while opening an IRL Performance Center to build community in LA.
Likeminded, Ghia evokes its founders’ childhood summers on the Mediterranean to sell NA apéritifs as a premium signifier of a slow lifestyle rather than a Type A sacrifice.

Takeaway: BFY bevs are complementing meaningful moments and worldbuilding their way to success, understanding legacy brands are built on cultural associations, not just ingredients. While the barrier to entry is lower, the bar for standing out has never been higher.

articles.headline: This Week in Charts: Are Prediction Markets Politically Biased?
articles.dek: Rule of 40 Ain’t What It Used To Be; Atoms keep winning; AI Has Come For Call Centers, After All?
articles.summary: Prediction markets called Brazil’s election weeks early, and an NBER study finds almost no partisan bias in them. Plus: why the Rule of 40 no longer tracks software valuations.

cover.alt: A ballot being dropped into a ballot box

blocks.text: By Moses Sternstein

Earlier this week, Flávio Bolsonaro secured a surprise first-round victory in the Brazilian presidential election. Or maybe it wasn’t a surprise. Charts knows next to nothing about Brazilian politics, so we really couldn’t say.
If you take a gander at the prediction markets, however, it appears as though Bolsonaro’s win was at least somewhat surprising, but not too surprising:

After pacing as a long shot for most of the year, odds began to turn in Bolsonaro’s favor in August, and by the second week of September, he was already the favorite. Unsurprisingly, Bolsonaro’s odds for winning the presidency have since skyrocketed, after the recent first-round win.

Whatever the surprise, prediction markets were early and right on this one by ~3 weeks. The outcome of the election is apparently consequential for financial markets too, judging by MSCI’s Brazil ETF, which jumped ~15% after the news of Bolsonaro’s first-round win. To be fair, the ETF also started climbing back in August (when Bolsonaro’s Kalshi odds began to turn), but not nearly as steeply or as uniformly. In other words, it seems fair to conclude that prediction markets had this one first.

All of this was a somewhat longwinded segue to some recent research that purports to show that prediction markets are actually pretty good at elections, or at least, they don’t demonstrate much partisan bias.

Prof. Zitzewitz published some preliminary findings in an NBER working paper that aggregated over 100 years’ worth of prediction markets (albeit with most of the sample coming recently) looking for evidence of over-pricing along various dimensions, including demographics and political affiliation. The premise of the study is that any bias would show up as outsized returns (either positive or negative) for whichever attribute(s) prediction markets systematically over- or underrated. That makes sense: if, e.g., prediction markets consistently underrate female candidates, then taking the “over” on female candidates would be a winning strategy (reflected by a positive coefficient).
As it turns out, the evidence of bias is pretty much non-existent:

This chart summarizes a subset of the results, and among political affiliation, gender, color, or age, there is not a single dimension where the return coefficient was above or below zero by an amount that exceeded the standard error—the only exception is for non-US elections, where prediction markets appear to reflect some bias in favor of right-leaning candidates (i.e. the coefficient is negative because markets overrate their chances), albeit over a much smaller sample. Even there, however, the 95% confidence interval indicates that the bias is not statistically significant.

Elsewhere, the results suggest a small (statistically insignificant) bias in favor of women and non-white candidates, and against older candidates, but when it comes to partisanship, the coefficient is a bare 0.03.
Take that for what you will, but the results imply that when it comes to elections, prediction markets are pretty good at leaving their biases at the door.
Rule of 40 Ain’t What It Used To Be

For years, the Rule of 40 was considered a lodestar for techco performance. The idea was to create a single metric that would enable comparisons across fast-growing companies at various stages of their lifecycle, where very rapid, and very unprofitable, growth was expected early, and less rapid, but more profitable, growth was expected as companies mature.

The Rule of [X] part is determined by summing revenue growth with profit margins, and if the number was 40 or higher, you were in good shape. So a company with 100% revenue growth, and -60% margins, was still winning because 100 + (-60) = 40, i.e. Rule of 40 on the nose... whereas 150% growth with -150% margins, clocking in at Rule of 0, would be less impressive (despite the faster growth).
Given that Rule of 40 is supposed to be a good thing, it’s odd to see these two things happening at once: public software cos are raising their Rule of X, while multiples are in steady decline:

With some fits and starts, the median Rule of X for public software has risen from ~17% to ~23% over the past ~3 years, with the steepest upward inflection beginning early 2025... just when revenue multiples began their precipitous decline.
Here’s another way of looking at it: the correlation between Rule of X and multiples (on a rolling basis) turned sharply south and eventually negative:
Again, it’s a weird thing. If Rule of X is a good thing, then an improving Rule of X should correspond to better multiples, and not the other way around.

So, what’s going on? The most likely explanation for why Rule of X is weakening as a signal has to do with the component parts: growth and profitability. As laid out in State of Markets, public (and private) techcos responded to post-ZIRP regime change by trading growth for profitability. What that means is that Rule of X is rising, but increased margins are doing most of the work, while growth makes a relatively smaller contribution.

But when it comes to multiples, investors put more of a premium on the latter than the former, so even if the Rule of X number is high, if growth has slowed substantially, multiples compress accordingly.
If you break techcos into their Rule of X buckets, you can see that revenue growth is just a much stronger factor than the combined Rule of X score:
Mind the different scaling on both axes, but the general idea is pretty clear: higher growth companies tend to have higher multiples than lower growth companies with an equivalent Rule of X.

In fact, for Rule of 20 all the way to Rule of 40, most companies are clustering in the same range between 5-10x EV/NTM sales—and it’s only the fastest growers (and really the ones with perceived tailwinds at their back, i.e. cyber and observability) that fetch a premium multiple.

The point here is pretty straightforward: in this brave new world for techcos, Rule of 40 just isn’t as useful anymore as a performance benchmark. The SaaS-Prove-It regime is okay with profitability, but it really likes growth, and if you’ve got a lot of the former, but not much of the latter, then the market isn’t very impressed, Rule of X be damned. If you’ve got both, then that’s all the better, but there aren’t too many of those.
Atoms keep winning, but what about everyone else?
Speaking of performance metrics where the headline picture may be obscuring some parts of what lies below, consider the recent downturn in the breadth of positive earnings revisions:

When breadth is positive (as it’s been since July of ‘25), that means earnings revisions are relatively broad-based... and when it’s negative, it means the good news is limited to a narrower subset of companies.
While revisions breadth is still positive, things have narrowed recently, with the implication that analyst optimism is training its fire, more so than before.
And where, might you ask, does even-more-optimism still abound? It’s really only in two sectors: energy and tech, but more specifically hardware, not software:

For the year, earnings revisions have been positive across the board (outside of utilities), but for Q3, the story is different: Energy improved, Tech improved—driven almost entirely by semis and hardware, with only the slightest uptick for software—and Financials improved modestly, as well, but every other sector experienced a downward revision from analysts. 2027 is a similar story: Energy, Hardware and Semis are the clear analyst winners, while the rest of the market, not so much.
In other words, expectations are that profits will continue to flow to Atoms, substantially more so than Bits.
AI capex shows no signs of slowing—if anything, the industrial backlog is increasingly broad-based:
As per the ISM, the share of industrial industries reporting a higher order backlog is now ~60%, which is the highest it’s been since pandemania.
At the same time as spending on the infra layer keeps piling up, there is some evidence that spending on everything else—while still high—is beginning to taper:

According to Carlyle’s private portfolio company data, shipments of AI hardware are still climbing at their exponential pace, while the “other side of the AI spend coin,” i.e. growth of the broader category of tech-spend, has leveled off at ~30%.

30% growth is pretty high—and much higher than before—but growth does not appear to be accelerating any longer, which is again, not the case when it comes to hardware. The implication is that after a year of better than expected results for pretty much everyone, that upside surprise may be narrowing.

Put another way, while the AI buildout keeps embiggering, that hasn’t changed expectations for how those benefits may flow through to the rest of the ecosystem—the epic run on atoms is picking up speed, even as it runs ahead of the field. Those unchanged-to-downwardly-revised forward estimates for everyone outside of AI infra are backed up by some hard data, as well, insofar as broader IT spending, while still growing, does not appear to be accelerating.

Of course, the fact that analysts have made upward revisions to their estimates for most of the year means that they’ve gotten this “wrong” before, but for now, consensus is signaling that the AI buildout will stay in the driver’s seat, even more so than before.
AI Has Come For Call Centers, After All?

While the broader evidence of the AI Jobs Apocalypse remains weak to non-existent—and indeed, there’s evidence that AI has increased demand for technical and hard-hat roles—there is some data that shows at least one “AI exposed” category is taking it on the chin: call centers.
According to data from Revelio, global call-center employment has gone sharply negative, after more than a decade of fairly consistent growth:

To be fair, growth began slowing when interest rates went up, which is slightly before GPT was released into the wild... but the downtrend has steepened substantially since then, and has accelerated of late.
Indeed, while lower-middle-income countries were relatively insulated from the downturn through most of 2024, even there growth has gone negative:

While higher-income countries went negative in 2022, lower-middle income countries stayed positive for another ~2 years. But, as of Q4’25, call center employment growth has gone negative everywhere, even in the poorest countries.
And lest one think that the downturn isn’t AI-driven (or specific to call centers), that too does not appear to be the case:
Outside of China, interestingly enough, call center employment has lagged the broader category of white-collar service work in every major non-US market for call centers.

Could there be other reasons for below-trend call center employment, besides AI? Probably, but call centers were always expected to be a likely target of substitution, so it seems reasonable to conclude that AI is the driver here. In the US, at least, the good news is that unemployment has been relatively stable, suggesting that the people who used to work in call centers appear to have found employment elsewhere... but changes are definitely underway, and one would expect more to come.
Source: a16z — https://www.a16z.news/p/this-week-in-charts-are-prediction
